output.headline: Rambert turns It’s a Sin into a dance piece rooted in club joy
output.standfirst: Exclusive: Rambert releases a trailer for its dance adaptation of Russell T Davies’s series about friendship amid the 80s Aids crisis, built around the ‘extraordinary freedom’ of clubbing
output.bodyHtml:
Russell T Davies’s award-winning series It’s a Sin is getting a new life as a dance piece, with a trailer released on Monday ahead of an opening at Aviva Studios in Manchester in February. The series follows young gay friends finding friendship amid the Aids crisis in 1980s London.

“We had a few approaches, but a lot of people wanted to make it a musical, which made my heart sink slightly,” said Davies. “I always imagined an aria between those two women on the seafront at the end and I thought: ‘Oh, that could be so terrible!’” Dance, he said, felt different: “It felt so original and so pure. The story distils down to these emotional moments that are going to be done so beautifully on stage.”

The idea came from Benoit Swan Pouffer, artistic director of Rambert, which marked its centenary this year with a commitment to reaching new audiences, partly by reinventing familiar titles, as in its dance version of Peaky Blinders. “Dance needs to be democratised and this is the way to do it,” said Pouffer, who is choreographing It’s a Sin.

Davies has a cameo in the trailer. His own dance career peaked with a performance for Princess Diana with West Glamorgan youth theatre (she told him he should continue to “Dance, dance, dance!”), but the dancefloor has always been an inspiration to him. “They’re such potent places, so loaded with potential.” Davies spent many nights in the clubs of Manchester’s Canal Street, watching lives play out to music. “Those dancefloors were places of such extraordinary freedom,” he said. “Especially in the 80s, with that layer of secrecy. That’s where you’d be out – you might not be out at home – becoming the person you aspired to be.”

Pouffer has seen the dance world’s losses from the Aids epidemic first-hand. “I had friends and colleagues who left us too early,” he said. Dancing in the US in the mid-90s, he saw as much stigma about HIV and Aids in the dance world as anywhere else. “There was shame, it was hidden. Even Alvin Ailey, that’s not what we said [that he died of an Aids-related illness] when he passed. Even now there is still a stigma,” said Pouffer. “The trauma, you put it in a little capsule and you don’t talk about it. Now we have this young PrEP generation who don’t know how traumatic it was. The closest they can think of is Covid,” he suggested. “Remember in the beginning when we didn’t know anything about the virus?”

Pouffer also wants to convey the excitement and creative spark of the era. “The fashion, the music, the dance of the 80s, it was one of the peaks of history,” he said. Video and narration, with scripts by Kaite O’Reilly, will help tell the story. Davies is an executive producer, as are Pet Shop Boys, whose title song will feature alongside an original soundtrack by Roman GianArthur.

Davies was turned down by all the major UK networks when he originally pitched the TV series, before Channel 4 eventually commissioned it. “It was simply an assumption that it would be miserable, even when they had the first script to read,” he said.

The series went on to be a huge hit. “Not a week goes past without someone stopping me in the street,” said Davies. Yet it was hard to celebrate, “because no matter how proud we were, it’s a story that’s founded on a lot of deaths”.

There is “a great heaviness at the heart of it, a great sadness and loss,” he continued. “But we told it with joy and vigour and life. The most important thing is to remember the life that those people had, not the death … I think the show worked because it turned around and said: ‘Hey, we loved those boys. Remember the love.’”

  • It’s a Sin is on tour from 16 February to 13 November 2027
